findings.title: paddedInLength reaches bit-width-sensitive LessEqThan without a bit-width constraint
findings.evidence: paddedInLength is a free input signal (sha.circom:97) that is only tied to inBlockIndex by the equality paddedInLength === inBlockIndex * 512 (line 111) and then fed directly into LessEqThan(maxBitsPaddedBits) at line 126 (bitLengthVerifier.in[0] <== paddedInLength) with bitLengthVerifier.out === 1 at line 128. LessEqThan/LessThan are only sound when both inputs fit in maxBitsPaddedBits bits, but no Num2Bits/range constraint is applied to paddedInLength, so it can be a field element near p (e.g. p-512 for the small negative length -512·k). Because the comparison arithmetic is done modulo p, such a value makes paddedInLength + 2^n - (maxBitLength+1) wrap to a small non-negative number, so out === 1 is satisfied even though the value is out of range. The matching negative witness inBlockIndex (which also satisfies line 111) is then passed to the final-block selector as arraySelectors[k].index <== inBlockIndex - 1 (line 175/289). ItemAtIndex (array.circom) also feeds this value to LessThan without a bit-width constraint, so the out-of-range index is accepted; no eqs[i] matches any small i, CalculateTotal returns 0, and every out[k] becomes 0, letting a malicious prover produce a valid proof whose SHA256 output is the all-zero 256-bit array for an arbitrary input. Scope note: only the standalone SHA256 template is affected; EmailVerifier's AssertZeroPadding prevents the end-to-end attack.
